findings.title: Negative slice start raises ValueError in Django, not a handled pagination error
findings.body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]`). The inline comment claims "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", which is false: Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects negative indices with `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` Every other paginator in this file guards this with `raise BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. The result is an unhandled exception and a 500 response that is trivially triggered by any client passing a cursor such as `-5:0:0`, i.e. a cheap error/DoS vector on the audit log endpoint.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate datetime columns, but is used with order_by="-datetime"
findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `math.floor(value)/math.ceil(value)` on the raw attribute and `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value, i.e. it only works for numeric keys (it is a copy of `Paginator`, not `DateTimePaginator`). The audit-log endpoint instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"` on `AuditLogEntry.datetime` (a DateTimeField). `build_cursor` calls `key(results[0])`, so `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, and on a follow-up request `build_queryset` injects an integer into `WHERE "datetime" <= %s`, comparing an int against a timestamp column. Any request to the new code path fails with a 500 or a database error.

findings.title: BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets, producing inconsistent cursors
findings.body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes `BasePaginator.get_result` so that a negative forward offset is silently clamped to 0 instead of surfacing an error. Two problems: (1) an invalid/garbage cursor now returns page-1 data as if it were valid, masking client bugs; (2) the raw negative `offset` is still passed on to `build_cursor` and still used in the `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check further down, so the drop-extra-row logic and the generated next/prev cursor offsets no longer correspond to the rows actually fetched. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still handed to Django and will raise. If clamping is desired it should be applied consistently (and the invalid case rejected with `BadPaginationError`).

findings.title: organization_context.member may be None, causing a 500 on the audit log endpoint
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` unconditionally whenever `is_superuser` is false. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` for callers that are not org members — notably org auth tokens / integration tokens and staff or superuser-flagged users accessing an org they do not belong to — so the expression raises `AttributeError` and turns a previously working GET into a 500. This runs for every request, not just when `optimized_pagination=true` is passed.

findings.title: "Advanced pagination" gate is not an admin check
findings.body: The comment says the feature is enabled for "authorized administrators", but the gate is `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. `request.user.is_superuser` is the raw DB flag and bypasses Sentry's required active-superuser/elevated-session check (`is_active_superuser(request)`), and `has_global_access` is true for ordinary members in open-membership organizations. So the out-of-bounds pagination path (negative offsets, no `BadPaginationError` guard) is reachable by regular org members and by superuser-flagged sessions that have not elevated. Feature flags that relax pagination bounds should be gated on an explicit permission check, not on these two signals.

findings.title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint query parameter
findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including the negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` are added with no test coverage in this PR. Both are trivially broken (negative slice raises in Django, `get_item_key` cannot handle datetimes) which a single endpoint test with `?optimized_pagination=true` would have caught.

findings.title: Set keys switched to sorted sets without renaming, breaking rolling deploys with WRONGTYPE
findings.body: `span-buf:s:{...}` keys change type from Redis SET to ZSET (`p.zadd` here, `zcard`/`zunionstore`/`zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua, `p.zscan` in `_load_segment_data`) while keeping the exact same key names. During a rolling deploy (and for up to `redis_ttl` = 1h after it) old SET keys written by the previous version still exist; `zadd`/`zcard` against them return `WRONGTYPE`, which aborts the Lua script and raises out of `p.execute()`, crash-looping the consumer. Old pods still running will likewise get `WRONGTYPE` from `sadd`/`sscan` on the new ZSET keys. The key prefix needs a version bump (e.g. `span-buf:z:`) so the two formats cannot collide.

findings.title: zunionstore uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting timestamp scores
findings.body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key`) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. Any span payload present in both source zsets — which happens on duplicate deliveries / reprocessing of the same span — gets its score set to the sum of the two `end_timestamp_precise` values, roughly doubling it. Since the score is used as the eviction ordering key for `zpopmin`, such a span becomes effectively un-evictable while legitimate newer spans are dropped instead. Pass `AGGREGATE MIN` (or MAX) explicitly to keep scores meaningful.

findings.title: Eviction limit hard-coded at 1000 while max_segment_spans config is now dead
findings.body: The new eviction (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`) hard-codes the segment span limit in Lua, while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` which, after the removal of the count check in `_load_segment_data`, is no longer referenced anywhere. Operators changing `max_segment_spans` now silently get no effect, and the two values disagree (1000 vs 1001). The limit should be passed to the script as an ARGV, or the unused parameter removed.

findings.title: Span eviction is now silent: no metric or log when spans are dropped
findings.body: The removed block in `_load_segment_data` emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged when a segment exceeded the span count limit. The replacement — `zpopmin` inside add-buffer.lua — drops spans with no counter and no log, so oversized-segment truncation becomes invisible in production and silent data loss cannot be detected or quantified. The script should return the number of evicted members so the consumer can emit a metric.

findings.title: Redirect-chain limit silently lowered from 10000 to 1000
findings.body: The loop bound was changed from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000` and the explanatory comment ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unannounced behaviour change: segment trees with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will no longer be joined into a single segment, producing split segments for deep traces. If the reduction is intentional it should be documented and the retained comment updated; the PR description mentions nothing about it.

findings.title: Module docstring/glossary still describes plain Redis sets
findings.body: The module docstring ("Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`", and the glossary entry "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") is now wrong: these keys are sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and the scoring is what drives the new eviction behaviour. Readers relying on the docstring will not know spans are evicted lowest-timestamp-first once a segment exceeds 1000 spans.

findings.title: Unguarded access to end_timestamp_precise can crash the consumer
findings.body: `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct indexing (unlike the neighbouring `val.get(...)` calls), so any message on the ingest-spans topic missing this field raises `KeyError` inside `process_batch` and kills the consumer rather than dropping/DLQ-ing the bad message. Given this is a newly required field, in-flight messages produced by older Relay versions would take the consumer down.
